title: Living ashtpadi 2
hookLine: the Name as a companion, not a charm

lines: A LUCKY COIN, A CHARM, A PHRASE.
SAY IT, AND THE BAD THING GOES?
READ IT AGAIN: WHO'S WITH YOU.
cards: A lucky coin in a pocket. A charm hanging from a rearview mirror. A phrase muttered before a free throw.

People everywhere keep little things that are supposed to make bad stuff not happen. It's easy to hear the second ashtpadi of Sukhmani that way: say the Name, and the bad thing goes away. But read it again.
Not one of its pictures is about the road disappearing. The darkness is still dark. The heat is still hot.
The door still shuts. What changes is who's with you.

teach.h: THE SALOK, THE DOOR, THE ROAD.
teach.b: Gather the second ashtpadi together. The salok: the breaker of the humble's pain, the protector of those with no protector, and Nanak coming to the shelter.
The first stanza: where no mother, father, child or friend can go, the Name goes with you. The road stanza: food, light, a known face, shade and rain.
All through, the key word is sang: with, together, in company. The Name goes sang, with you. That's the difference between a charm and a companion.

teach.h: A CHARM IS A TOOL; A FRIEND IS PRESENT.
teach.b: A charm is a tool: you use it to get an outcome, and if the outcome doesn't come, the charm failed. A companion is a presence: they don't stop the storm, they sit through it with you.
Sikh teaching is wary of using sacred words as magic. Gurbani speaks sharply about empty ritual and outward show, as the next ashtpadi will show, and simran is meant to be remembering, not a spell.
So when a Sikh family reads Sukhmani by a hospital bed, the hope is not mainly a bargain, read this and the scan comes back clear.
The hope is that the person in the bed, and everyone in the room, isn't alone in what comes.

teach.h: FOR BAD DAYS AND GOOD ONES.
teach.b: That makes the Name for good days and bad ones alike.
A charm is for emergencies. A companion is for every day: the commute, the kitchen, three in the morning.

how: Sikhs often read the second ashtpadi of Sukhmani with someone who is ill or grieving, and understand simran as remembering God in company with the Name, not as a spell to change outcomes.

o: a song sung together at day's end
a lucky charm kept close for protection

games.q: the second ashtpadi, gathered — tap the pairs.
p: the breaker of the humble's pain
the Name goes where family can't

s: in the second ashtpadi, saying the Name makes the hard road disappear
every picture keeps the road; what changes is who's with you.
Gurbani speaks sharply about empty ritual
simran is meant as remembering, not a spell.
the Name goes sang, with you.

games.q: a friend asks whether reading Sukhmani by a hospital bed is a way to guarantee good news. what does the second ashtpadi suggest?
o: yes, it works like a charm.
it offers company through what comes, not a guaranteed outcome.
it only matters if the news is bad.
games.why: the Name in ashtpadi 2 is a companion: it goes with you where no one else can, through the dark and the heat.

practice: Notice that you're alone with this lesson, or alone in your head even with people near, and instead of filling the quiet, sit in it and breathe slowly.
If you pray, say Waheguru once, not to make anything happen, just to notice company; if you don't, notice that this moment is being lived, and you're here in it.

wordCard.voice: Sang, with, together: Sukhmani's second section in daily life, the Name not as a charm that stops the storm, but as a companion who goes with you through it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sang, with, in company; how the Name goes with you in the second ashtpadi.

carryVoice: Your line: never alone. The door still shuts, and someone still comes through with you. Four hundred forty-five, and counting.
